Key PHP 8.5 Features for Your Rewrite

The biggest game-changer for simplicity in PHP 8.5 is the Pipe Operator (|>). It stops you from having to read code "inside-out" and lets you chain actions together logically.

Here are practical "Before & After" examples tailored for a typical service website.

1. Cleaning User Input (e.g., from a "Request Service" form)
Imagine a user enters their phone number as "(555) 123-4567 " and you need to store it as just numbers.

The Old "Inside-Out" Way (Harder to Read): You have to read this from the inside bracket outwards to understand what's happening.

PHP
// Old Way
$raw_phone = "(555) 123-4567 ";
$clean_phone = strip_tags(trim(str_replace(['(', ')', '-', ' '], '', $raw_phone)));

// What is happening?
// 1. str_replace runs first
// 2. trim runs on that result
// 3. strip_tags runs on that result
The Modern PHP 8.5 Way (Simple & Clear): Use the pipe operator (|>) to pass the value down a chain of tasks. It reads like a set of instructions.

PHP
// New PHP 8.5 Way
$raw_phone = "(555) 123-4567 ";

$clean_phone = $raw_phone
    |> str_replace(['(', ')', '-', ' '], '', ...) // Step 1: Remove symbols
    |> trim(...)                                  // Step 2: Remove outer whitespace
    |> strip_tags(...);                           // Step 3: Remove any HTML tags

// Result: "5551234567"
// The (...) is a placeholder for the value coming from the previous step.
Why it's better: It's perfectly clear what happens step-by-step. It's easier to write and much easier for someone else to understand later.

2. Working with Lists (e.g., Service Areas or Testimonials)
Let's say you have a list of service areas and you want to display the main one (the first) and the furthest one (the last) on your homepage.

The Old Way (Clunky): Using older functions like reset() and end() moves an internal pointer inside the array, which can lead to weird bugs if you aren't careful.

PHP
// Old Way
$service_areas = ['Monteregie', 'Montreal'];

$primary_area = reset($service_areas); // Moves pointer to start
$furthest_area = end($service_areas);  // Moves pointer to end
The Modern PHP 8.5 Way (Efficient & Safe): Use the new native functions. They don't mess with internal pointers and do exactly what their names say.

PHP
// New PHP 8.5 Way
$service_areas = ['Monteregie', 'Montreal'];

$primary_area = array_first($service_areas); // "Downtown"
$furthest_area = array_last($service_areas);  // "Monteregie"
Why it's better: The intent is instantly clear by reading the function name. It's simpler and less error-prone.

3. Handling Page URLs
If your site needs to look at the current URL to decide which "active" tab to highlight in the navigation menu.

The Old Way (Loose & Messy): Using parse_url() gives you a simple array that you have to manually check parts of.

PHP
// Old Way
$current_url = "https://plumbingservices.com/services/drain-cleaning?source=ad";
$url_parts = parse_url($current_url);
$path = $url_parts['path'] ?? '/'; // Have to manually handle missing keys
The Modern PHP 8.5 Way (Object-Oriented & Clean): Use the new URI Extension. It gives you a powerful object to work with.

PHP
// New PHP 8.5 Way
$uri = Uri::new("https://plumbingservices.com/services/drain-cleaning?source=ad");

$path = $uri->getPath(); // "/services/drain-cleaning"
$is_secure = $uri->isHttps(); // true
Why it's better: It uses a modern, object-oriented approach that is more robust and easier to read than dealing with raw arrays.

General Modern Best Practices to Apply
Beyond the specific 8.5 features, apply these rules to make your whole codebase better understood.

Use Type Hinting Everywhere: Don't let PHP guess what kind of data it's using. Be explicit. This prevents bugs and makes code self-documenting.

Bad: function getQuote($plumbingIssue) { ... }

Good: function getQuote(string $plumbingIssue): float { ... }

Separate Logic from Views: Don't mix your PHP business logic with your HTML.

Do this: Have a PHP file that gets data (e.g., fetches list of services from a database).

Then do this: Have a separate HTML template file that simply loops through that data and displays it. This makes changing the design vastly simpler without breaking the code.

Use Descriptive Names:

Bad: $d = get_data();

Good: $availableServices = fetchServicesFromDatabase();
